title: The older Reformed meant justifying grace only
source_text: XVII. Imo illos ipsos ex vetustioribus qui dissentire videntur, revera non dissentire puto. Quum enim contra Scholasticos contendunt gratiam non esse habitum in animam infusum, manifeste de gratia justificante agunt. Itaque mens eorum simpliciter non est, nullos habitus virtutum in fidelium animas a Deo per Spiritum sanctum infundi, & ejusmodi habitus nullibi gratiae nomine designari: sed hoc tantum, gratiam per quam in scripturis dicimur servari & justificari, in sanctis istis habitibus nullo modo consistere: sed per gratiam istam unice significari Dei misericordiam & benevolentiam. Cujus rei argumentum est, quod aliquando gratiam qua servamur, justificamur, imo & regeneramur, non tantum negant esse habitum & qualitatem infusam, sed quicquam in nobis creatum & inhaerens, uti de Polano supra retulimus. Et tamen idem Polanus in eodem capite agnoscit esse quandam gratiam inhaerentem, quae, inquit, est tum fides, tum gratia conversionis & regenerationis, quam gratiam Christi Redemptoris, item gratiam Christianam vocant. Adeoque quum negat gratiam regenerantem esse quicquam in nobis creatum & inhaerens, loquitur tantum de causa efficiente & impulsiva regenerationis nostrae, non de causa quam vocant Scholastici formalem.
pass_a_gloss: XVII. Nay those very ones from the older who seem to dissent, I think in reality do not dissent. For when against the Scholastics they contend that grace is not a habit infused into the soul, they manifestly treat of justifying grace. Therefore their mind is not simply, that no habits of virtues are infused into the souls of the faithful by God through the Holy Spirit, and that habits of this kind are nowhere designated by the name of grace: but this only, that grace through which in the scriptures we are said to be saved and justified, in no way consists in those holy habits: but that by that grace is solely signified the mercy and benevolence of God. Of which thing the argument is, that sometimes the grace by which we are saved, justified, nay and regenerated, they not only deny to be a habit and infused quality, but anything created and inhering in us, as we related above of Polanus. And yet the same Polanus in the same chapter acknowledges that there is a certain inhering grace, which, he says, is both faith, and the grace of conversion and regeneration, which they call the grace of Christ the Redeemer, likewise Christian grace. And so when he denies that regenerating grace is anything created and inhering in us, he speaks only of the efficient and impulsive cause of our regeneration, not of the cause which the Scholastics call formal.
pass_b_english: Thesis XVII. Indeed, I think that even those older writers who seem to disagree do not really disagree. When they argue against the scholastics that grace is not a habit infused into the soul, they are plainly dealing with justifying grace.

So their meaning is not, without qualification, that God infuses no habits of virtue into believers' souls through the Holy Spirit, or that such habits are never called grace. They mean only that the grace by which scripture says we are saved and justified does not consist in those holy habits at all, and that this grace means God's mercy and goodwill alone.

The proof is this. At times they deny that the grace by which we are saved, justified and even regenerated is a habit and infused quality, and they also deny that it is anything created and inhering in us, as we reported of Polanus above. Yet Polanus himself, in the same chapter, grants that there is an inhering grace. This, he says, is faith and also the grace of conversion and regeneration, which people call the grace of Christ the Redeemer, and likewise Christian grace.

So when he denies that regenerating grace is anything created and inhering in us, he is speaking only of the efficient and impelling cause of our regeneration, not of what the scholastics call its formal cause.
